output.name: Nasmi

anatomy.part: far end of the laid rope, where the twist still holds
the rope body near its tip, where the lay begins to loosen
the knot where the strands part, the brightest point of the fray
the end of the first loose strand, trailing down
a bend in the long lower strand
a second bend further along the same strand
the tip of a strand flung far to the east
the final hair of the outermost strand

output.myth: When Aun cut the string, the sky went up, and the dead went with it as kites. But the Unflown lies past where the wind comes back, and there the dead do not stay knotted. Mother Hesk counted them as they left, and the count was right, but what she could not count was the rope. Nasmi is a length of old rope, untwisted back to its fibres, each strand going its own road. The sailors who saw it in the south say the strands never reach one another again. Each one is a voice that goes on alone, thin and cold, singing in the tar-smelling dark. Ennu, who wrights kites from cloth and bone, once tried to lay the strands back. His hands cramped and he gave it up, and that is why the old women say: do not untwist what you are sad to lose. Keep your knots tied, and keep counting.
output.verse:
Hands untwist the rope,
each strand takes its own far road,
no knot remembers.

problems: The blind guess (a side-view fish or bird with a pointed head) does not match The Unlaid Rope. The blue silhouette reads as a long, thin, tapered band with a pointed tip at upper left, which is closer to a loose rope or strand than to a bird.

The blue contour is a real silhouette, not a copy of the gold lines: it runs beyond the gold skeleton at the upper-left twisted section and along the upper edge toward star 107089. That part is acceptable.

Star placement is only partly right. Star 2021 (the fray knot, near x=143, y=254) sits on the blue outline where the strands part, which is correct. Star 3781 (far end, near x=85, y=205) and star 122 (rope body near the tip, near x=180, y=240) are close to the upper-left twisted section. Stars 117689, 112405, 110256, 107089 and 104043 trace the lower and eastern strands, but the lower strand's bends are drawn as sharp angles rather than the gentle bends the labels describe.

The labels overlap each other and the figure: 'the knot where the strands part' collides with 'the rope body near its tip', and the lower labels run into the gold lines. This makes the drawing hard to read even where the geometry is right.
The figure is upright in the frame (rope end at upper left, strands trailing down and to the right), so orientation is fine.
judge.advice: Redraw so the silhouette reads unmistakably as a loose rope rather than a bird or fish. Keep the figure in its current upright orientation. (1) Upper-left: make the laid rope a tapered band from star 3781 (~85,205) down-right through star 122 (~180,240), with the twist visibly tightening near 3781. (2) Knot: put star 2021 (~143,254) exactly on the point where the band splits, the brightest point. (3) Lower strand: from 2021 draw a continuous, gently curved strand down to star 117689 (~213,375), then a smooth bend through star 112405 (~282,355) and a second smooth bend through star 110256 (~315,337), rising toward the east. (4) East strand: continue from 110256 up to star 107089 (~391,272) as a flung tip, then a thin hair out to star 104043 (~447,289). (5) Make the blue silhouette a filled, tapered rope shape along this path (not a thin outline that loops at the upper left), so it no longer resembles a pointed-head animal. (6) Move labels to non-overlapping positions with leader lines, keeping them off the figure. Gold lines should remain only as the skeleton through the key stars.
